course_description:
This course aims to provide students with foundational knowledge and skills relevant to the study of politics across the areas of Governance and Public Policy, Peace and Conflict Studies and International Relations. Before one can write well in politics, one must be able to read well. Thus, the course begins with consideration of the importance of critically reading texts in order to recognize both argument and underlying assumptions. Doing so requires acknowledgment of the open-ended or essentially contested nature of many of the concepts that are used in political discourse and analysis. Such recognition equips us to be informed readers and therefore more skilful analysts and writers in our chosen field. Through close reading of texts, interactive class exercises and a number of written assignments students will have the opportunity to build their analytical and writing skills in this field.

We begin the course by exploring the meaning of politics and the various approaches to its analysis across cultures and societies. We then investigate and critique fundamental concepts such as power, authority, and legitimacy; ideas and institutions; decolonisation and sovereignty; the state; and globalisation and global governance, drawing on examples from a range of social, political, and cultural contexts in the Asia Pacific region and beyond. Recognising that these concepts are pivotal in defining and shaping polity and political ordering within societies, a comprehensive understanding of them will enable students to analyse politics, political discourses, and the mechanisms and institutions through which political life is constructed and enacted at local, national, and international levels.

Through a dedicated writing workshop, the course also explores approaches, methods, and styles of political analysis and writing, supporting students in developing foundational skills for writing in politics.

assessment_details.task_description: This assessment requires students to write six reflective summaries of their learning due in Weeks 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, and 12. The first five reflections should draw on required readings and seminar discussions for the relevant week. The final reflective piece, due in Week 12, should reflect on students’ key learning across the course as a whole. This does not need to summarise each and every aspect of their learning, instead you may like to focus on your most notable learning, which may be about understanding a concept, theory or applying an analytical approach for political analysis. As a guide, each learning reflection should be a maximum of 300 words, except the final reflection which should be between 400-450 words. The first five reflections are worth 3 marks each (i.e. total 15 marks), and the final reflection is worth 5 marks. A very short writing for example, less than 150 words receives a 0 mark. This task is not a summary of the readings. Rather, it is an opportunity for students to demonstrate their learning through reflective writing. Written feedback will not be provided for every submission; however, each submission will be checked to ensure the task has been completed and that students are eligible to receive the mark. Deadlines: First learning reflection: 7 August 2026 Second learning reflection: 14 August 2026 Third learning reflection: 28 August 2026 Fourth learning reflection: 11 September 2026 Fifth learning reflection: 18 September 2026 Final learning reflection: 23 October 2026 Weekly learning reflection: Marking criteria Weekly reflections are designed to encourage critical engagement with course material and to facilitate connections between readings, seminar discussions, and broader political debates. Marking criteria Demonstrates thoughtful reflection on key learning. Engages critically with course readings and seminar discussions, showing understanding of relevant concepts, theories, or political issues. Writes clearly and correctly, using appropriate grammar, punctuation, and spelling. Meets the required word limit and submission requirements. To achieve high marks, students should move beyond description and demonstrate critical reflection, analysis, and engagement with the week's learning. Submissions under 100 words will receive a mark of zero. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly reference any use of AI or MT in each instance. assessment_details.title: Analytical op-ed with a theoretical appendix
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment requires you to write an analytical op-ed suitable for publication in a major public-facing outlet (such as The Conversation, Australian Outlook, Foreign Policy, or The Interpreter). It must address a contemporary political issue related to one of the following themes: Power, authority and legitimacy Democracy and its threats You should choose a case or event in relation to the above topic in the past two years. The assessment has two parts; both must be submitted as a single document. The first part is an analytical op-ed (15 marks). In this part, present a clear and persuasive argument aimed at public audiences. Use accessible, non-academic language, and develop a focused analysis and argument. Where you draw on evidence or scholarship, weave it naturally into the text. This is how good political journalists and policy analysts often write. Where citations are necessary, embed them as hyperlinks within the text. Your goal is to communicate a complex political idea in a way that is engaging, accurate, and analytically sharp. The second part is a short theoretical appendix (10 marks). In this part you must explain the academic foundation of your argument in the op-ed. Identify the key political concepts and theoretical perspectives used, and briefly explain how those concepts connect to or inform the position you took. Include appropriate citations and references. The appendix must provide the conceptual reasoning behind your argument in the op-ed, not a summary of commentary or literature review. While the analytical op-ed is written for a public audience, the appendix demonstrates your capacity to connect your argument to relevant scholarly debates. The word count for both components combined is 1,500 words. You should allocate approximately 1,000–1,100 words to the first part and 400–500 words to the second part. Citations and references are excluded from the word count. This assessment is designed to develop students’ ability to translate complex political theory and concepts into analytical writing for wider audiences, while maintaining conceptual rigour and analytical depth. An example and marking criteria will be available on the course Blackboard site. assessment_details.title: Essay planning and research strategy
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment requires you to develop a clear plan and research strategy for your final essay. It has two parts; both must be submitted as a single document. Part One: Essay plan (5 marks) In this part, you will produce a short essay plan of approximately 400 words. The plan should briefly outline the background to the issue or problem your essay will address, clearly state your research question, identify the key concepts and theories you will use in the final essay, and present a provisional argument or thesis statement. Your argument may evolve as the essay develops, but you should still aim to express it as clearly as possible at this stage, since it will guide your research and writing. Part Two: Source identification and evaluation (10 marks) This part assesses your ability to find, evaluate, and select sources for your essay. You will search for material using two different methods: UQ Library search A generative AI platform (e.g., Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, and so on) From each method, produce a list of seven sources, for a total of fourteen. Any source suggested by a generative AI platform must be independently verified. To do so check that it exists, that the citation details are accurate, and that it examines what the AI claims it does. After reviewing all fourteen sources, select the eight most relevant and useful for your essay. Write a justification of up to 1,000 words explaining why you chose these eight, how you assessed their quality and credibility, and why they are a strong fit for your essay. This justification is not a review or summary of the sources themselves; it should demonstrate your ability to evaluate their relevance and suitability for your research. You may add further sources in the final essay as necessary. References are excluded from the word count. A list of essay questions will be available on the Blackboard site early in the semester. Students may also devise their own essay questions, provided they relate to one of the course topics. assessment_details.title: Research Essay (with a hurdle)
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment requires students to write a 3000-word essay based on their previously submitted essay plan. You should expand on the aims, argument, and methods outlined in your plan. The essay requires you to engage in further reading and research, drawing on both course materials and relevant academic literature on your chosen topic. When writing your essay, please ensure the following: Present a clear and well-structured argument that directly answers the essay question. Use appropriate scholarly sources and critically evaluate them. Build your own argument in response to the essay question, supported by this literature. Clearly explain your reasoning, showing how your conclusion follows from the arguments you present. Include relevant examples to support your analysis. Write clearly and concisely, using correct grammar and academic expression. Cite all sources accurately, using the recommended referencing style (APA 7th edition). Proofread your essay carefully before submission, and check your Turnitin similarity score. References are not included in the word count.
